title: DI fundamentals (IServiceCollection, constructor injection)
hook: ASP.NET Core ships a built-in dependency injection (DI) container. You register services in IServiceCollection at startup and receive them through constructor parameters — the container builds the object graph for you.

blocks.text: Dependency injection (DI) is a design pattern where a class receives its collaborators from outside instead of creating them with new. ASP.NET Core provides a built-in inversion of control (IoC) container backed by Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection. You register abstractions and implementations in IServiceCollection during startup (builder.Services), then the runtime resolves them when constructing controllers, minimal API handlers, middleware, and your own services. Constructor injection is the preferred style — the container picks the constructor with the most parameters it can satisfy.

entries.plainDefinition: Supplying dependencies to a class from outside rather than the class creating them.
entries.example: public OrdersController(IOrderService orders) — container injects IOrderService

entries.plainDefinition: The registration API used at startup to map service types to implementations and lifetimes.
The built service container used to resolve registered services at runtime.
Dependencies are supplied through the class constructor — the only injection style ASP.NET Core uses for framework activation.
entries.example: public sealed class OrderService(IEmailSender email) : IOrderService

blocks.text: Without DI, every controller would new up its own DbContext, HTTP clients, and loggers — untestable, tightly coupled, and impossible to swap implementations. The built-in container lets you register IOrderRepository once and inject it everywhere. Integration tests replace real services with fakes via WebApplicationFactory. Interviewers expect you to explain registration, resolution, and lifetimes — not just say 'use DI'.

blocks.title: Register abstractions, not concretions
blocks.body: Prefer builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>() over AddScoped<OrderService>(). Controllers and handlers depend on IOrderService — tests can substitute a fake without touching production code.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Register in Program.cs
items.body: Call Add* extension methods on builder.Services — map interface to implementation with a lifetime.

items.title: Build the provider
items.body: builder.Build() compiles the service descriptor table into an IServiceProvider (optionally validating the graph).

items.title: Request arrives
items.body: ASP.NET Core creates a scope (for web requests) and activates the endpoint target.

items.title: Constructor resolution
items.body: The container walks the dependency tree, constructing each type from the inside out.

diagram.title: DI registration and resolution flow
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  REG[IServiceCollection\nAddScoped IOrderService] --> BUILD[Build IServiceProvider]
  BUILD --> REQ[HTTP Request\ncreates scope]
  REQ --> CTRL[OrdersController ctor]
  CTRL --> SVC[OrderService ctor]
  SVC --> DB[AppDbContext ctor]
  DB --> DONE[Handler executes]

snippet.label: Register services and inject into a controller
snippet.explanation: AddDbContext registers a scoped DbContext. AddScoped gives one OrderService per request. The controller primary constructor receives IOrderService automatically — no [FromServices] needed on controllers.

snippet.label: Service with its own dependencies
snippet.explanation: OrderService depends on AppDbContext and ILogger<T>. The container resolves both when constructing OrderService, then injects OrderService into the controller. ILogger<T> is registered by the framework.

snippet.label: Manual resolution with GetRequiredService
snippet.explanation: CreateScope() is required for scoped services outside a request. GetRequiredService fails fast with a clear exception — better than null checks in production code.

snippet.label: ValidateOnBuild — fail at startup, not at first request
snippet.explanation: ValidateOnBuild compiles and validates the full dependency graph at startup. Enable in CI so misconfigured lifetimes never reach production. This is a diagnostics snippet — the failure happens before Kestrel binds a port.

blocks.title: ASP.NET Core DI vs NestJS vs Express
rows: None — manual require() or third-party libs

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Calling BuildServiceProvider() inside ConfigureServices — creates a second container and orphan scopes. Registering concrete types only so tests cannot substitute fakes. Using service locator pattern (injecting IServiceProvider everywhere) instead of constructor injection. Forgetting to register an interface — GetRequiredService throws at first request.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: enable ValidateOnBuild in CI pipelines — startup fails if the graph is invalid. Use dotnet-trace to capture service resolution during integration tests. Application Insights dependency tracking shows if your service layer is accidentally creating new HttpClient per call (missing IHttpClientFactory registration). Code review: grep for new OrderService() or new HttpClient() in application code — both indicate DI bypass. The built-in container is not as feature-rich as Autofac or Scrutor decorators, but it covers 95% of Web API needs and keeps startup fast.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Fast, zero extra packages, first-class ASP.NET support
No built-in decorators, limited conditional registration
Extra dependency, slower startup, testing complexity
Slightly slower startup in dev if overused

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying 'DI is just for testing' without explaining decoupling and lifetime management. Not knowing the difference between IServiceCollection (registration) and IServiceProvider (resolution). Claiming property injection works on controllers — ASP.NET Core only supports constructor injection for framework-activated types. Unable to explain why BuildServiceProvider() inside registration is an anti-pattern.

interviewTakeaways: IServiceCollection registers; IServiceProvider resolves — constructor injection is the only framework-supported activation style.
Register interfaces (IOrderService) not concretions — enables testing and swapping implementations without changing consumers.
Production tip: ValidateOnBuild true in CI; grep for new HttpClient() and new DbContext() in app code — both bypass DI.

60s: Register in builder.Services with AddSingleton/Scoped/Transient. Build creates IServiceProvider. Container walks ctor chain to resolve controllers and services. Prefer abstractions. ValidateOnBuild catches misconfigured lifetimes at startup.
Follow-up: when would you replace the built-in container with Autofac or Scrutor?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'just inject IServiceProvider everywhere' gets you rejected — that is service locator, not DI; dependencies should be explicit in constructors.
BuildServiceProvider() during registration creates a second container — orphan scopes and disposed DbContext bugs.
Strong answer: 'Register abstractions in IServiceCollection. Constructor injection only. ValidateOnBuild in CI. NestJS has similar IoC; Express requires manual wiring or awilix.'
introducedIn: ASP.NET Core 1.0 (built-in DI); ValidateOnBuild in generic host 2.1

jsTsCorrelations.note: NestJS registers providers in module metadata and injects via constructor — closest analog to ASP.NET Core DI. Scope.DEFAULT maps to singleton, Scope.REQUEST maps to scoped, Scope.TRANSIENT maps to transient.

Express has no built-in container. Common pattern: create services at startup, attach to app.locals, or pass via closure to route handlers. Equivalent to service locator — no lifetime enforcement, no graph validation.
